text: Lesson 26's connectivity sequence checks network, routing, firewall rules, DNS, and the listening port, and it will correctly say everything passes on a ticket that still doesn't work. A surprisingly large share of real deployment tickets turn out to be a genuine permission gap, where an app's identity or a user's role was never granted the right to do what it's trying to do.

Before touching a single role assignment, read the actual error text, because it almost always tells you which category you're in. Access denied, Forbidden, 403, or AuthorizationFailed means the request reached the resource and got actively refused — that's a permission problem. A connection that timed out or got no route to host, with no application response at all, is almost always a network or firewall problem instead.

That single distinction, an answer that said no versus no answer at all, is the fastest triage step available, and it's the one engineers skip most often under pressure, usually by assuming a denial means something about the network is misconfigured when it's saying the opposite. Once the error text confirms a permission problem, the next step is finding exactly which role or policy statement is missing, not just confirming that permissions are involved.

A real Azure error for a failed listKeys call names the exact denied action. From there: identify the identity making the call, list its current role assignments, compare that against what the action actually requires, and assign the specific role needed. The error almost always names the exact action denied, so there's rarely a need to guess.

Scope matters as much as the role itself. Granting Contributor on an entire subscription technically fixes the error, but it's the wrong fix — it's over-granting access that becomes its own security problem later. The right fix is always the narrowest role, at the narrowest scope, that satisfies the specific action the error named. Lesson 28 covers the decision that comes after any root cause is found: roll back, or fix forward.
